ACTRESS FALLS IN
THE RIVER.
Amusing Experience After a Rescue.
Miss Lloreen Hamilton, one of the pretty young actresses playing at the Waldorf Theatre in the "Gipsy Girl" company, has had an unpleasant, not to say dangerous, experience.

She was one of the party who yesterday visited the upper reaches of the Thames upon the invitation of Mr. William Armstrong, chairman of London Musical Productions, Ltd., and the accident happened when the steam launch carrying the party was between Hampton Court and Richmond.

To the music of the theatre orchestra several couples were dancing on the narrow deck, when one collided with the rail. The gentleman stumble, and the lady, Miss Lloreen Hamilton, fell head foremost into the river just as the gates of a neigh-
bouring lock were being slowly opened and the water rushing in.

Miss Hamilton disappeared from view for a moment, and there was a rush to the side, several male members of the party preparing to dive to her rescue. However, this was not necessary, for Mr. B. Blanchard was lowered into the water by means of a rope and managed to grasp Miss Hamilton as she reappeared.
Then the pair were drawn on board, the young actress being at once hurried into the cabin.

A difficulty, however, presented itself. While Miss Hamilton's clothing was drying in the stakehold what was she to wear? None of the other members of the party could spare any article of attire, there were no "props" on board, so what was she to do?

Eventually, however, one of the waiters remembered he had a spare suit on board. Would Miss Hamilton accept? Miss Hamilton had no choice, and so, in a waiter's dress suit she remained between decks until her own dress was again available.

ACCIDENT IN FLEET-STREET.

Just before ten o'clock yesterday morning, when Fleet-street was thronged with people, a somewhat alarming accident occurred. At the premises of Messrs. Carl Hentschel (Limited), process engravers, within a few yards of St. Dunstan's Church, a gang of men were engaged in installing safes and office furniture. Most of the work had been concluded, but a large wooden cabinet remained, which was too awkward to get up the stairs, and was therefore taken into the street, and "tackle" fixed at the third-floor window. It had been hauled as high as the second floor, where there was a hitch, and three men at the window above were leaning out, trying to ease it. Without the slightest warning, the whole of the window-sill and adjoining masonry, with the ropes holding the case and staging, gave way, and the men were dragged or fell a distance of some 40ft to the pavement.

Fortunately a fourth man on the ground saw what was happening, and warned a number of passers-by, who were able to jump aside clear of the falling masonry. It was at once seen that the men from above had sustained severe injuries. Robert Fitzgerald, who lives at Hoarssee-place, Old Ford, E., had fractured the right leg, and there were deep cuts on his head and face. The other two men, John Cassidy, of Spitalfields, and Thomas Jones, of Upper Clapton, were cut and bruised, and one appeared to have been badly injured internally. Doctors were summoned, and the three victims were conveyed to St. Bartholomew's Hospital on ambulances.

The foreman, who was inside the room at the moment of the accident, states that the cabinet being lifted was of no appreciable weight, a mere mass of light wood, which splintered with the fall. He noticed the cord fly into the air, heard a crashing noise, and saw the three men falling away from him. He managed to catch hold of one of them, and was almost dragged through the window before he was compelled to lose his bold.

LENS REVEALS SECRETS.
What is the fastest thing in the world that the human race has ever invented?

The steel projectile of a 12in. gun. No human eye could possibly follow its flight, for it is hurried through the air at the rate of twenty-five mile a minute and reaches the mark ahead of its own sound.

Yet Captain F. J. Behr, of the United States Coast Artillery Corps, has actually developed a system by which it is possible to photograph the flight of these projectiles. Captain Behr was assisted in his experiments by Engineer J. A Wilson.
We can see to-day, in photographs taken by Captain Behr, things which the human eye has never seen before.

The whole wonderful story is set out very full in this month's issue of "McClure's Magazine," which details how Captain Behr, after years of experiments, was at last able to obtain a series of rapid photographs showing a 12in battery at work.
He had invented an electric device for working the shutter of the camera, and these pictures were taken in about one five-thousandth part of a second.
Some of the increments and decrements of time involved in taking these photographs are as small as one ten-thousandth part of a second.
SEEN LEAVING MUZZLE.

It is now possible to photograph the swiftes mortar projectiles travelling at tremendous velocities, in almost any desired position. You can actually see the projectile leaving the muffle of the mortar.
In the photograph it looks as though it is stationary. In reality, it was "snapped" when travelling 1,500 miles an hour!
In one of the photographs reproduced in today's Daily Mirror the smoke cone from the muffle of the mortar looks like a great fluffy powder-puff. This effect has never been seen by the human eve.
The "powder puff" hides the projectile which has just issued from the mouth of the mortar a the rate of 1,500 miles an hour.
It is interesting to note that no sound is heard until the fourth phase in the travels of a projectile has been recorded by Captain Behr's camera.

Sometimes, through Captain Behr's invention, the hurting projectile is itself the photographer for in passing out of the great gun barrel it breaks a length of piano-wire stretched across the mouth of the gun, and thus it automatically closes an electric circuit that actuates the mechanism of the camera. LENS REVEALS SECRETS.
What is the fastest thing in the world that the human race has ever invented?

The steel projectile of a 12in. gun. No human eye could possibly follow its flight, for it is hurled through the air at the rate of twenty-five miles a minute and reaches the mark ahead of its own sound.

Yet Captain F. J. Behr, of the United States Coast Artillery Corps, has actually developed in a system by which it is possible to photograph the flight of these projectiles. Captain Behr was assisted in his experiments by Engineer J. A. Wilson.
We can see to-day, in photographs taken by Captain Behr, things which the human eye has never seen before.

The whole wonderful story is set out very fully in this month's issue of "McClure's Magazine," which details how Captain Behr, after years of experiments, was at last able to obtain a series of rapid photographs showing a 12in. battery at work.
He had invented an electric device for working the shutter of the camera, and these pictures were taken in about one five-thousandth part of a second.
Some of the increments and decrements of time involved in taking these photographs are as small as one ten-thousandth part of a second.

It is now possible to photograph the swiftest mortar projectiles travelling at tremendous velocities, in almost any desired position. You can actually see the projectile leaving the muzzle of the mortar.
In the photograph it looks as though it is stationary. In reality, it was "snapped" when travelling 1,500 miles an hour!
In one of the photographs reproduced in today's Daily Mirror the smoke cone from the muffle of the mortar looks like a great fluffy powder-puff. This effect has never been seen by the human eve.
The "powder puff" hides the projectile which has just issued from the mouth of the mortar at the rate of 1,500 miles an hour.
It is interesting to note that no sound is heard until the fourth phase in the travels of a projectile has been recorded by Captain Behr's camera.

Owing to the great velocity of gun projectiles it is, indeed, practically impossible for an observer even when stationed near the target to see them as they approach. And the projectile actually hits the target before the observer hears the sound of the discharge.

Sometimes, through Captain Behr's invention, the亨ting projectile is itself the photographer, for in passing out of the great-gun barrel it breaks a length of piano-wire stretched across the mouth of the gun, and thus it automatically closes an electric circuit that actuates the mechanism of the camera. A safety lock for railway carriages, patented about a month ago, has brought a fortune to a railway signalman named George Caswell, of Churchroad, Newport, Monmouthshire.
One of the principal railway companies has, it is stated, offered £19,000 for the invention and the offer has been accepted.

Mr. Caswell built a model of a train in brass, and showed that a rod running the whole length of the train on the top of the carriages, and controlled by a lever on the engine, could effectively lock the doors of all the carriages in the train, and thus the guard could unlock them by a lever in his van. The rod is connected with a simple apparatus at the foot of each door.

THE KING AND BOY HERO.
Medal Presented by His Majesty for Bravery in Welsh Disaster.
The little Welsh lad, Tom Lewis, who showed such heroism on the occasion of the disaster at Newport Docks in July last, received the Albert medal yesterday at the hands of the King.
The lad was conducted to the Thyron Room at Buckingham Palace, where the Home Secretary presented him to the King, and gave a summary of the official account of Tom Lewis' gallant act.
His Majesty shook hands cordially with the boy and expressed the great pleasure that it gave him to receive him.
The heroic act thus honoured was the saving of a man's life under conditions of great difficulty and danger.

When a trench collapsed at Newport Docks a number of men were pinned down by great beams, and to rescue one of these men the aid of a slim boy who could slip through a narrow gap between the beams was required.

Tom Lewis volunteered, and for two and a half hours he worked with hammer and chisel down in the darkness of the trench, to release the captive. Every moment there was the danger of some further collapse, and eventually the shifting of the sand prompted the watchers above to haul the boy up again. The man below afterwards worked his way out with a saw the boy had left him.

Prior to receiving Tom Lewis the King conferred some of the honours bestowed on the occasion of his Majesty's birthday, and Sir Ernest Shackleton introduced the members of his Antarctic expedition to receive their medals.
After the investiture the King left for Chester on his way to visit the Duke and Duchess of Westminster at Eaton Hall.
His Majesty arrived at Chester at 4.50 p.m., and was met by the Duke of Westminster and the mayor and corporation, who presented an address. He afterwards motored with his host to Eaton Hall.

The citizens of Chester displayed bunting and decorations in the streets the King passed through, and great crowds watched his Majesty's car pass.

The Prince and Princess of Wales left King's Cross at 5.30 yesterday afternoon for Brockett Hall on a visit to Lord Mount Stephen.
